title: York man was held at gunpoint over incorrect Flock hit. Sheriff blames illegal tag cover

reading.body:
This is a false positive in an automated licence plate reader, and the failure is not the misread itself but what the misread was allowed to trigger. The system matched a plate to a stolen vehicle record and that match was treated as sufficient grounds for an armed stop, with no step in between where a person checked the alert against the plate in front of them. The error was a single character, which is the ordinary failure mode of optical character recognition under poor conditions, and it is exactly the kind of error a verification step exists to absorb.

Catching it would have required the deputy to confirm the alert independently before drawing a weapon, which is the practice the vendor itself says should apply. The gap is between what the system is designed to produce, a candidate match, and how its output was used, as a confirmed fact about a person. Nothing in the deployment appears to have enforced that distinction at the point of enforcement.

What is not established is the cause. The claim that an illegal tinted plate cover produced the misread comes from the sheriff's office, and its judgement that the deputy acted reasonably is that office's own characterization, not an independent finding. The reporting does not establish what the reader actually did or why.

reports.title: York man was held at gunpoint over incorrect Flock hit. Sheriff blames illegal tag cover

summary: Steven Melvin, 42, of York County, South Carolina, was held at gunpoint for over five minutes after a Flock Safety license plate reader misread the first letter of his plate and matched his BMW to a similar stolen vehicle. The sheriff’s office later said an illegal tinted plate cover caused the error and called the deputy’s actions reasonable. Flock said alerts should be independently verified before enforcement.
